question_text: A 55-year-old construction worker falls off a 2-story scaffolding and injures his back. His coworkers bring him to the urgent care clinic within 30 minutes of the fall. He complains of left lower-limb weakness and loss of sensation in the right lower limb. He does not have any past medical history. His vital signs are stable. A neurologic examination reveals a total loss of motor function when testing left knee extension, along with the left-sided loss of light touch sensation from the mid-thigh and below. There is a right-sided loss of pin-prick sensation of the lateral leg and entire foot. At this time of acute injury, what other finding is most likely to be found in this patient?

                    ### Question
                    A 55-year-old construction worker falls off a 2-story scaffolding and injures his back. His coworkers bring him to the urgent care clinic within 30 minutes of the fall. He complains of left lower-limb weakness and loss of sensation in the right lower limb. He does not have any past medical history. His vital signs are stable. A neurologic examination reveals a total loss of motor function when testing left knee extension, along with the left-sided loss of light touch sensation from the mid-thigh and below. There is a right-sided loss of pin-prick sensation of the lateral leg and entire foot. At this time of acute injury, what other finding is most likely to be found in this patient?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Left-sided numbness at the level of the lesion
opb. Intact voluntary anal contraction
opc. Left-sided extensor plantar response
opd. Right-sided loss of proprioception and vibration sensation
ope. Left-sided spastic paralysis below the lesion

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient presents with neurological deficits following a fall, indicating possible spinal cord injury. The left lower-limb weakness and sensory loss in the right lower limb suggest an upper motor neuron lesion, likely due to damage at the lumbar or sacral level. The presence of left knee extension weakness and sensory deficits aligns with the possibility of left-sided spastic paralysis below the lesion, which is consistent with upper motor neuron involvement. Therefore, the most likely finding in this patient is left-sided spastic paralysis below the lesion, supported by the consensus that such injuries can lead to upper motor neuron signs. Other options, such as intact voluntary anal contraction or right-sided loss of proprioception, do not align with the expected findings in this scenario.
